deep.reconstruction:
The page is part of a table of quadratic residues of primes p. It is the 5th leaf of the table, since the 5 at top right is a folio number. Each entry gives a prime p, a sign, and the least positive residues a with (a/p) = +1.

Layout convention (consistent across pages):
- p ≡ 1 (mod 4) (here 277, 281, 293): a '+' is written above p (−1 is a residue) and '∓' before the list. Only residues in 1..(p−1)/2 are listed, since a and p−a have the same character.
- p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (here 283, 307, 311): a '—' is written above p (−1 is a non-residue) and '+' before the list. All residues in 1..p−1 are listed, since a and p−a have opposite characters.

Contents of the page:
- Lines 1–3 finish the list for p = 271, begun on the previous page, from 125 up to 268. The residue 241.242 is written as a superscript correction.
- p = 277: list in 1..138. It has 69 entries, as it should.
- p = 281: list in 1..140, 70 entries.
- p = 283: full list in 1..282.
- p = 293: list in 1..146, 73 entries.
- p = 307: full list.
- p = 311: list running to 195, continued on the next page up to 300.

Non-trivial feature: in the lists for 277, 281 and 293 Gauss drew vertical strokes at the octant points p/8, p/4 and 3p/8.
- 277: strokes after 34, after 69, and after 102 (p/8 = 34.6, p/4 = 69.25, 3p/8 = 103.9).
- 281: strokes after 35, after 70, and after 101 (35.1, 70.25, 105.4).
- 293: strokes after 36, after 73, and after 109 (36.6, 73.25, 109.9).

The resulting residue counts per octant (my count) are:
- 277: 19, 17, 19, 14
- 281: 21, 19, 11, 19
- 293: 18, 23, 18, 14

Splitting the half-range into quarters and octants is exactly what is needed to evaluate the Dirichlet/Gauss class-number expressions as character sums over intervals. Examples are h(−4p) = 2·Σ_{n<p/4}(n/p) for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and analogous octant sums for discriminant −8p. These are consistent with genus theory: 2·(R−N) on (0,p/4) gives 6, 20 and 18, which are ≡ 2, 0, 2 (mod 4) for p ≡ 5, 1, 5 (mod 8). That they equal the class numbers is my inference and is not checked here.

For p ≡ 3 (mod 4), the half-range count also checks out against h(−p) = Σ_{n<p/2}(n/p) / (2 − (2/p)) (my verification). The listed residues ≤ p/2 number:
- 271: 73 (68 from the previous page + 5 here), giving Σ = 11 = h(−271).
- 283: 75, giving Σ = 9 = 3·h(−283).
- 307: 81, giving Σ = 9 = 3·h(−307).
- 311: 87, giving Σ = 19 = h(−311).

The page itself contains only the residue lists and octant markers; no class numbers are written.
errors: No genuine errors found in the residue lists after spot-checking dozens of entries by reciprocity and checking the totals: 277 has 69, 281 has 70, 293 has 73, 307 has 153, and 283 has 141 if both 264 and 265 are read.

The blots in the 307 list are deletions of erroneously entered non-residues. They sit after 28, after 71, after 129, after 150, at 263, between 264 and 269, and after 295. In each gap I checked, every number is a non-residue mod 307. So Gauss caught and blotted his slips.

p = 307: the superscript '146' and '285' are insertions, not replacements. Both 146 and 148 are residues mod 307, and so are both 284 and 285. Only with both pairs present does the count reach 153 and the half-range count reach 81.

results.what: Table of least positive quadratic residues for primes 271–311. Only the half-range is listed for p ≡ 1 mod 4, the full range for p ≡ 3 mod 4, with the sign of −1 indicated.
results.modern_name: Table of quadratic residues (Legendre symbol table)
results.usually_credited_to: Such tables are standard. Gauss refers to residue tables in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), and Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus (1839) is related.

results.what: Division of the residues of 277, 281 and 293 into octants (0,p/8), (p/8,p/4), (p/4,3p/8), (3p/8,p/2) by vertical strokes, evidently to count residues per interval.
results.modern_name: Interval character sums of the Legendre symbol, and class-number formulas for h(−4p), h(−8p) as sums over quarter/octant intervals
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet (1838–40), with Gauss's unpublished 'De nexu inter multitudinem classium...' (Werke II), which already contains such interval-count expressions.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a computational residue table, accurate and self-corrected. The octant markings point to Gauss's well-documented (posthumously published) work linking class numbers to residue counts in intervals of length p/4 and p/8. That work is already attributed to him in Werke II, so the page adds only a minor working document.
